title: Weekly Top Five: Who Trained Your Appetites?
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: This is Anthony Bradley's weekly curated digest of five articles, each with his own editorial summary, followed by a short closing reflection. The items cover John Berger's idea of attention as a moral act, the high price of nonfiction books and how publishers shape reader behaviour, a Columbia student column on consent and the limits of a permission ethic, a PsyPost report on how long it takes Christians to feel forgiven after wrongdoing, and a PsyPost report on teen boys who follow Andrew Tate. Bradley highlights details such as average nonfiction hardcover prices and the finding that parental messages about toughness outweighed following Tate as a predictor of traditional masculine beliefs. His closing note ties the set together: the internet is not more powerful than a father's voice, and people choose with appetites that someone else trained. Filed under Family because the closing emphasis is on how boys learn manhood at home. The Tate study is expanded as its own entry.
points: Berger's claim that attention is a moral act is paired with the warning that platforms increasingly do our remembering for us.
The nonfiction item argues publishers help create the sales slump by pricing readers out and underpromoting nonfiction.
The consent column's point is that consent tells us only whether something was allowed, not whether it was good.
The forgiveness study finds that repentance rises before felt forgiveness, though the authors caution this does not mean forgiveness is earned.
Bradley's closing synthesis is that boys learn manhood at home before they meet it online, so a father's voice outweighs the internet's.
quotes: Berger insisted that “to see is always to give shape to the world,” that perception “is always contingent on where you stand and who is standing with you.
Non-fiction books are too expensive. This is 100% true folks! Tajja Isen interrogates a common explanation for declining nonfiction sales: fatigued readers are turning to escapism.
When you have an industry that prices audiences out of a genre, they’ll soon find the data that prove they never wanted it anyway.
Consent only allows us to know if something was allowed, not if something was good.

However, having parents communicate to them about the importance of being big and tough was by far the biggest predictor in any given model, with about twice or three times the explanatory power of following Tate.
The internet, for boys, is not more powerful than his father’s voice. A boy hears, sees, and learns what a man is at the dinner table and at home before he hears it on a phone.
Lastly, people do choose, yet they choose with eyes, appetites, and preferences that are guided by someone else who showed them the way.
